1.title: The Sprint and the Scrum Events
1.text: Welcome to Module 6: The Sprint and the Scrum Events. You now know the team. This module shows the rhythm they work in. You will learn what a Sprint is, the four events inside it, the timeboxes you must memorize, how to choose a Sprint length, and when a Sprint can be cancelled.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. State the purpose and maximum length of a Sprint. Name the four events with their purpose, participants, sequence and timebox. Give three benefits of a timebox. Choose a suitable Sprint length. Give an example of inspecting and adapting at each event. And say when a Sprint can be cancelled, and by whom.

1.title: Case Check-In: How Long Should a Sprint Be?
1.text: At RideLoop, the team chose two-week Sprints four months ago. Now Grace Whitfield suggests six-week Sprints, because, in Grace's words, the product is complex. Grace also wants to skip the Review and the Retrospective in a busy Sprint, to save time. As Scrum Master, you prepare your answers. By the end of this module, you will know exactly what to say, and which Guide statements to point to.

1.title: The Sprint
1.text: Sprints turn ideas into value, and they set the pulse of Scrum. A Sprint is a fixed-length event of one month or less. A new Sprint starts immediately after the last one ends. All the work necessary to reach the Product Goal, the events included, happens inside Sprints. You can think of each Sprint as a short project. For the exam: never longer than a month, never stretched to finish, and never shortened because the work is done early.

1.title: The Five Events
1.text: There are five events. The Sprint is the container, and inside it sit four more: Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. Each one is a formal chance for the team to inspect and adapt. So if a team skips an event, or changes it, that chance is lost. That is your answer to Grace's wish to skip the Review and the Retrospective. Events create regularity and minimize the need for meetings that Scrum does not define, and ideally they happen at the same time and in the same place, which keeps things simple.

1.title: The Four Events: Purpose and Participants
1.text: Here is the purpose and the participants of each event. Sprint Planning starts the Sprint and sets out the work. The Scrum Team takes part, and guests may come for advice. The Daily Scrum is for the Developers: they check progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjust their plan. The Sprint Review inspects the outcome of the Sprint with key stakeholders, and decides future adaptations. The Retrospective is for the Scrum Team, to plan ways to raise quality and effectiveness.

1.title: Timeboxes and Sequence
1.text: Memorize these timeboxes, for a one-month Sprint. Sprint Planning: eight hours. Daily Scrum: fifteen minutes. Sprint Review: four hours. Sprint Retrospective: three hours. They are maximums. For shorter Sprints, Planning, Review and Retrospective are usually shorter, but the Daily Scrum is fifteen minutes whatever the Sprint length. The order is Planning, then the Daily Scrums, then the Review, and finally the Retrospective. The Review is second to last, and the Retrospective concludes the Sprint.

1.title: During the Sprint
1.text: During the Sprint, four rules apply. No change is made that would endanger the Sprint Goal: the goal is stable, though the plan can change. Quality does not decrease, so the Definition of Done is never lowered to save time. Refinement of the Product Backlog continues as needed. And scope can be re-discussed with the Product Owner as understanding grows, as long as the Sprint Goal stays intact.

1.title: What Is Not in Scrum
1.text: Some practices you may meet are not in Scrum. This slide is beyond the Guide, but it follows from the rules. Extending a Sprint because the team is late. Shortening a Sprint because work finished early. A Sprint zero before the real Sprints. A hardening or release Sprint. A gap between Sprints. All the necessary work happens inside Sprints, one after another, and the next one starts at once. If an exam option adds any of these, it is wrong.

1.title: Benefits of a Timebox
1.text: The learning objective asks for at least three benefits of a timebox. These go beyond the Guide. Regularity: everyone knows when events happen. Focus: a fixed limit stops endless discussion. Faster decisions: a deadline forces one. Limited waste and risk: a wrong direction is found early. A rhythm of inspection: each timebox ends with a look at the result. And fewer unplanned meetings, because the events minimize the need for extra ones. Name at least three.

1.title: Choosing a Sprint Length
1.text: How long should a Sprint be? The Guide sets one boundary: one month or less. It also gives the reasoning. A very long Sprint can leave the goal out of date, and let complexity and risk grow. Shorter Sprints give more learning cycles and limit the cost and effort at risk. The Guide names no preferred length. Two weeks is a popular practice, not a rule. So, for Grace's six-week idea, the answer is simple: not allowed.

1.title: Factors in the Choice
1.text: When choosing a length, weigh these factors. This slide goes beyond the Guide. How fast feedback is needed, or how fast the market changes: shorter. How uncertain or risky the work is: shorter, so the team learns sooner. How long a usable Increment takes: choose a length in which the Definition of Done can be met. Stakeholder availability: choose a length that lets them attend the Review. Event overhead: very short Sprints mean frequent events. Team experience: try a length for a few Sprints, then keep it stable. The rule of thumb: pick the shortest length in which the team regularly finishes a usable Increment, and keep it fixed.

1.title: Inspect and Adapt at Each Event
1.text: The learning objective asks for an example of inspecting and adapting at each event. These examples go beyond the Guide. In Sprint Planning, the team inspects the Product Backlog, its capacity and its past performance, and adapts by forming a Sprint Goal and selecting what fits. At the Daily Scrum, the Developers inspect progress and adapt the plan for tomorrow. At the Review, the team inspects the Increment and adapts the Product Backlog. At the Retrospective, it inspects its way of working and adopts an improvement.

1.title: Cancelling a Sprint
1.text: When can a Sprint be cancelled? Only when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. And that decision belongs to the Product Owner alone; others may raise the concern. Being late, finding the work harder, losing a Developer, or a manager wanting something else are not reasons to cancel. In those cases the Developers and the Product Owner negotiate scope, protecting the Sprint Goal. The earlier edition of the Guide had a longer section on cancelling; the current one keeps only the condition and the authority.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. Fixed length, one month or less, and a new Sprint starts at once. The maximum timeboxes for a one-month Sprint: eight hours, fifteen minutes, four hours and three hours. The Review is second to last, and the Retrospective concludes the Sprint. Skipping an event loses a chance to inspect and adapt. Only the Product Owner cancels, and only if the goal is obsolete. And the Guide calls them events, not ceremonies; it uses the word meetings only for meetings outside Scrum. Refinement is an ongoing activity, not an event.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. The Sprint is a fixed-length container of one month or less. The four events are Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Review and the Retrospective. The timeboxes for a one-month Sprint are eight hours, fifteen minutes, four hours and three hours. Shorter Sprints limit risk and give more learning. During the Sprint, protect the goal and the quality, and renegotiate scope. Only the Product Owner cancels. Now test yourself.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Two days before the end of Sprint eight, the Developers realize that three items will not be finished. They ask to extend the Sprint by three days. What is the best answer? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Sprints are fixed length, so a Sprint is not extended. The unfinished items return to the Product Backlog, and the Developers and Maya can renegotiate scope. Cancelling is only for an obsolete Sprint Goal.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A new Scrum Team that Lakeshore Transit is starting for another product wants a four-week Sprint zero to set up the environment and gather all requirements before its first Sprint. How should the Scrum Master respond? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. All necessary work happens within Sprints, and a separate preparation phase is not part of Scrum. The team starts small. The Guide does not require two weeks either.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Halfway through the Sprint, the Developers conclude that the work is harder than expected and that the Sprint Goal may be missed. What is the best action? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. The Developers and the Product Owner negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog without affecting the Sprint Goal. Quality is not lowered, the Sprint is not extended, and cancelling is for an obsolete goal only.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which set of maximum timeboxes is correct for a one-month Sprint? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A: Planning eight hours, Daily Scrum fifteen minutes, Review four hours, Retrospective three hours. Option B swaps the Planning and Review times. The other two options invent different numbers.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which of these is a benefit of a timebox? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. A fixed limit keeps discussion focused and forces decisions, which limits waste and risk. It does not guarantee that every item is finished, it does not replace inspection, and because it is a maximum, it is not extended whenever the team wants more time.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: A. Sprints are fixed length. Question two: C. All necessary work happens inside Sprints, and there is no Sprint zero. Question three: D. Negotiate scope without affecting the Sprint Goal. Question four: A. Eight hours, fifteen minutes, four hours, three hours. Question five: C. Focus and forced decisions limit waste and risk. That completes Module 6. Next, Module 7 takes Sprint Planning in depth.
